extracted.intended_audience: general readers, media scholars, and writers interested in satire and satirical news
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit standards for producing and evaluating satirical news (deadpan/parody news articles, video parodies, and related formats) as exemplified by The Onion's practices and controversies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Straight-faced (deadpan) presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: "the straight-faced manner in which The Onion reports non-existent events, happenings and ideas has resulted in third parties mistakenly citing The Onion stories as real news."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presenting parody in a deadpan news voice increases comedic effect and plausibility but carries the risk that readers, other media outlets, or officials may treat stories as factual. Examples include multiple instances where outlets or individuals republished or cited Onion stories as real.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base satire on obvious, intuitive truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Rensin's observation that the publication must work from "obvious, intuitive truth—the kind necessary for any kind of broadly appealing humor."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective satire often amplifies or skewers an obvious kernel of social/political truth. This approach tends to create broadly appealing jokes but can also produce predictable slants or ideological readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of political slant and perceived advocacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commentators have characterized the publication as producing "biting, leftist op-ed pieces through its presentation of satire news," while others criticize it for advocating particular positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirical outlets should recognize how selection of targets, framing, and recurring themes can create a perceived political stance or advocacy. This affects reception, credibility with different audiences, and potential critique that the outlet isn't 'neutral' satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurring caricature can shape real-world perceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Onion's long-running caricature of Joe Biden as a blue-collar "creepy but harmless uncle" is believed to have benefited the real Joe Biden's public image; former editor Joe Garden later expressed regret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using recurring characters or repeated caricatural portrayals can have unintended political or social consequences beyond the joke (e.g., shifting public perception of real figures). Writers should consider long-term effects of repeated portrayals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signal parody clearly enough to avoid harmful misinterpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple incidents where The Onion's pieces were mistaken for real news (e.g., republishing by foreign newspapers, social-media shares by public figures) demonstrate this risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While realism increases comedic payoff, creators should balance plausibility with sufficient cues (context, framing, disclaimers when appropriate) to reduce the risk of real-world confusion, misinforming the public, or causing unintended fallout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider offensiveness and potential for public harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples such as the tweet calling 9-year-old Quvenzhané Wallis a derogatory term and the Subway September 11 parody ad generated widespread anger, apologies, and internal dispute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirists must weigh shock value against ethical considerations and likely public harm. Offensive jokes can provoke backlash, damage reputation, and prompt formal apologies; editorial oversight and sensitivity to targets (especially minors, victims) are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and regulatory considerations when parodying official symbols or institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. Presidential Seal dispute: the White House assistant counsel sent a cease-and-desist about use of the presidential seal; The Onion replied arguing its use was parody and requested permission under the executive order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using protected symbols, seals, or closely imitating government/institutional marks, creators should understand legal constraints, be prepared for challenges, and consider formal clearance or defense strategies (and the difference between parody and implying sponsorship/approval).

rubrics_metrics.name: Format-fidelity: mimic real formats to heighten parody
rubrics_metrics.description: The Onion produced many series that parody specific formats (TED Talks, ESPN, Facebook, C-SPAN, Vice, WIRED Explains, morning talk shows, recipe/cooking videos, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faithfully reproducing the style and conventions of a target format (tone, visuals, structure) strengthens the parody by creating recognizability and contrast. However, high fidelity can also increase risk of being mistaken for the real thing and may require clearer signaling or disclaimers in certain contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire can be prescient; plausibility matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The Onion has on occasion predicted real-life incidents (e.g., pieces that preceded product launches or later news stories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounding satire in plausible futures or logical extensions of present trends can make jokes feel prophetic and increase impact. Writers should be mindful that plausible exaggerations may later be read as prediction rather than satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational ethics and labor practices influence credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage of the writers' unionization, criticism about employee benefits and health insurance, and publicized staff disputes are part of The Onion's history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsroom employment practices, treatment of staff, and institutional ethics affect both internal morale and external reputation. Publishers of satire should attend to fair labor practices and transparency, as these can become part of how audiences evaluate the outlet's legitimacy and moral standing.
